title: Structures, Unions, Enums & Bit-fields
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs probe whether candidates understand composite C types, memory layout, and safe patterns for overlapping storage and packed data.

phases.goal: Establish what structs, unions, enums, and bit-fields are and how they are declared and accessed.

must_hit.point: A structure is a contiguous block of memory containing a sequence of named members of potentially different types.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says struct groups heterogeneous members under one namespace in contiguous memory.

must_hit.point: A struct tag alone requires the struct keyword on every declaration; typedef creates an alias so the keyword can be omitted.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts struct Point p1 with typedef'd Point p2.

must_hit.point: Members are accessed with '.' ; C99 designated initializers map values by name, and unspecified members are zero-initialized.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions .x/.y form and that omitted fields become zero.

must_hit.point: A union allocates enough memory for its largest member; all members start at the same address (offset 0) and writing one overwrites another.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes overlapping storage / hotel-safe analogy and shared address.

must_hit.point: Enums assign names to integer constants; by default the first is 0 and later ones increment by 1, with explicit values allowed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives STATE_IDLE=0, STATE_RUNNING=1, STATE_ERROR=-1 style example.

must_hit.point: Bit-fields let you specify how many bits a member occupies within an integer word, e.g. packing fields into a single 16-bit word.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes : width syntax and packing enable/interrupt/mode/reserved/ready into one word.

probes: What is a struct, and how does a union differ from it in how members are stored?
Why wrap a struct declaration in typedef, and what do C99 designated initializers buy you?

hints.1: Think about whether members sit side-by-side or share the same bytes.
hints.2: Struct = contiguous named sequence; union = size of largest member, all at offset 0.
hints.3: Also cover tag vs typedef, '.' access, designated initializers zeroing unspecified members, enum defaults, and bit-field widths.

phases.goal: Explain layout rules, pointer access, self-reference, type punning, tagged unions, and flexible array members.

must_hit.point: Struct size is rarely the sum of member sizes: the compiler inserts padding so members meet alignment; overall alignment is the largest member alignment and total size must be a multiple of that.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains padding after char before int, trailing padding for arrays, and _Alignof.

must_hit.point: For struct { char a; int b; char c; }, sizeof is typically 12 bytes, not the naïve 6; reordering to int then two chars yields sizeof 8 bytes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States bad_layout ~12 and good_layout 8 with trailing pad to multiple of 4.

must_hit.point: Pass structs by pointer (const if read-only) to avoid copy; ptr->member is sugar for (*ptr).member.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States always pass by pointer and shows p->x equivalent to (*p).x.

must_hit.point: A struct cannot contain an instance of itself but can contain a pointer to its own type; the struct tag form is required because a typedef alias is incomplete until the closing brace.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions infinite size vs fixed-size pointer and Node *next with tag.

must_hit.point: In C (C99/C11), reading a different union member than last written is defined type punning of the overlapping object representation; in C++ reading an inactive member is Undefined Behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts C-sanctioned punning with C++ strict-aliasing UB.

must_hit.point: Because a union does not track the active member, pair it with a tag (tagged union / variant); C11 anonymous nested struct/union projects members into the enclosing scope.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows DataType tag plus anonymous union, and Player.x without intermediate name.

must_hit.point: A C99 flexible array member is an incomplete array as the last member; sizeof of the struct excludes it, and you malloc sizeof(struct) plus room for elements.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows int data[]; and malloc(sizeof(Vector) + 100 * sizeof(int)).

probes: Why might sizeof(struct { char a; int b; char c; }) not be 6, and how does reordering change it?
How do you pass a large struct into a function, and how can a struct form a linked-list node?

hints.1: Alignment forces gaps; pointers avoid copying whole structs.
hints.2: Walk bad_layout vs good_layout sizes, then -> vs (*p)., then self-pointer with tag.
hints.3: Add type-punning C vs C++, tagged unions/anonymous members, and FAM last-member + malloc sizing.

phases.goal: Surface packing, performance, and portability choices the file calls out.

must_hit.point: __attribute__((packed)) or #pragma pack drops padding (e.g. network_header size exactly 5 bytes) but can force slow byte-by-byte access on architectures without unaligned loads.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States save memory vs severe performance penalty / shifting instructions for int.

must_hit.point: Order members largest-alignment-first to minimize padding; on a 64-bit system the Trace example shrinks from 24 bytes to 16 bytes when reordered.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares Trace 24 vs TraceOptimized 16 and saved 8 bytes per instance.

must_hit.point: Bit-field ordering is implementation-defined (e.g. GCC on x86 often LSB-to-MSB); for portable exact hardware register maps prefer bitwise operations over bit-fields.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns never rely on bit-fields for portable hardware bit positions.

probes: When would you pack a struct, and what do you give up?
Why might you reorder struct members or avoid bit-fields for hardware registers?

hints.1: Padding helps the CPU; packing matches wire/hardware layouts.
hints.2: Packed: exact size (e.g. 5) but unaligned cost; reorder largest-first to cut waste.
hints.3: Cite Trace 24→16 and that portable register mapping should use bitwise ops, not bit-fields.

phases.goal: Apply offsetof, tagged-union dispatch, and self-referential pointers in concrete interview-style tasks.

must_hit.point: Byte offset of a member without an instance: offsetof(type, member) from <stddef.h> (null-pointer cast resolved at compile time).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names offsetof and compile-time null-pointer technique.

must_hit.point: A tagged Value with ValType plus anonymous union of int/float is switched on the tag before reading the matching member.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes switch on v->type then v->i or v->f.

must_hit.point: A binary tree node holds payload plus struct TreeNode *left and *right (pointers to own type, not embedded instances).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Completes right as struct TreeNode *right matching left.

probes: How do you get a member's byte offset inside a struct without creating an instance?
How would you safely print a variant that may hold int or float?

hints.1: There is a standard macro for member offsets.
hints.2: offsetof from stddef.h; for variants, store an enum tag beside the union.
hints.3: offsetof(type, member); switch on type then read the active field; tree children are struct TreeNode *.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Default layout inserts padding for aligned, fast, fault-free access; packed attributes/#pragma pack yield exact sizes (e.g. 5-byte header) needed for hardware/network but may force byte-wise loads and severe slowdowns where unaligned access is unsupported.

tradeoffs.topic: Member order for space vs naïve declaration order
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Declaring largest-alignment members first minimizes padding (good_layout 8 vs bad_layout typically 12; TraceOptimized 16 vs Trace 24 on 64-bit), at the cost of possibly less natural field ordering in source.

tradeoffs.topic: Bit-fields vs bitwise operations for hardware registers
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Bit-fields concisely pack sub-word widths into an integer word, but ordering is implementation-defined; for portable exact register maps, use explicit bitwise operations instead.

tradeoffs.topic: Passing structs by value vs by pointer
tradeoffs.strong_answer: By-value copies every byte and is expensive for large structs; pass a pointer (const if read-only). Returning by value may get RVO, but an out-pointer remains a common explicit C idiom.

gotchas.trap: Assuming you can read/write structs directly to disk or network as raw byte streams.
gotchas.correction: Padding bytes hold garbage and layout varies by compiler and architecture; serialize fields explicitly or use a packed, agreed wire format carefully.

gotchas.trap: Expecting sizeof(struct { char; int; char; }) to be 6.
gotchas.correction: Alignment padding typically makes it 12; reorder members (int then chars) to get 8 including trailing padding.

gotchas.trap: Reading an inactive union member the same way in C and C++.
gotchas.correction: In C, type punning via a different union member is defined; in C++, reading an inactive member is Undefined Behavior.

gotchas.trap: Putting two enums in the same scope that both define IDLE (or similar).
gotchas.correction: C enum constants leak into the surrounding scope; prefix enumerators (e.g. STATE_IDLE).

gotchas.trap: Using bit-fields to map exact portable hardware register layouts.
gotchas.correction: Bit-field order is implementation-defined (LSB-to-MSB vs MSB-to-LSB); use bitwise operations when portability matters.

gotchas.trap: Embedding a struct instance of the same type inside itself, or using a typedef name inside its own incomplete definition.
gotchas.correction: Only a pointer to the type is allowed (fixed size); use the struct tag inside the definition because the typedef alias is not complete until the closing brace.
